fieldFixes.summary: Daniel Howe and Helen Nissenbaum of New York University released TrackMeNot, a free Firefox extension that periodically sends randomised 'ghost' queries to search engines so that a user's real searches are harder to profile. Its authors cited the U.S. Justice Department's 2005 subpoena to Google for search records and the New York Times coverage of AOL's release of search logs. By their count it had passed 350,000 downloads by 2009; a 2010 study showed that a search engine holding only a short history of a user's queries could break its privacy guarantees using off-the-shelf machine-learning classifiers.

fieldFixes.title: Netflix's 'anonymous' ratings are shown to be re-identifiable
fieldFixes.summary: Arvind Narayanan and Vitaly Shmatikov of the University of Texas at Austin presented a statistical attack on the Netflix Prize dataset, which held movie ratings of about 500,000 subscribers with names replaced by numbers. They calculated that eight ratings (two of which may be wrong) with dates accurate to 14 days single out 99% of records. As a proof of concept they compared the public Internet Movie Database ratings of about 50 users with the dataset and matched two of them to their Netflix records with high statistical confidence, uncovering what the authors called apparent political preferences and other potentially sensitive information. In March 2010, after FTC staff raised the research with the company, Netflix suspended plans for a second prize dataset.

fieldFixes.summary: In July 2009 Christopher Soghoian and Sid Stamm built a prototype Firefox add-on that added 'X-Do-Not-Track: 1' and 'X-Behavioral-Ad-Opt-Out: 1' headers to outgoing web requests, as an alternative to the per-company opt-out cookies that were erased whenever users cleared their cookies. In mid-July Soghoian pitched the header at a meeting and conference call organised by the Future of Privacy Forum; none of the advertising firms showed interest, and after joining the FTC a couple of months later he decided against adding the header to his TACO opt-out add-on. After FTC chairman Jon Leibowitz revived the 'do not track' idea in July 2010, the header approach displaced a 2007 advocacy proposal for an FTC-compiled Do Not Track list, and W3C worked on it as the DNT standard until 2019.
fieldFixes.significance: It moved the tracking choice from one cookie per ad company to a single signal a person's own software sends to every site: the one-bit ancestor of machine-readable personal terms.
fieldFixes.locationNote: Soghoian's account does not say where the meeting was held; the coordinates are FPF's home city, Washington, D.C. (city centre, approximate).
